newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Rubber-Prices seen steady to easier in quiet trade.
newsitem.headline: Rubber-Prices seen steady to easier in quiet trade.

text.p: Southeast Asian rubber prices are seen remaining steady to easier this week while Malaysian SMR20 grade prices may have to be adjusted lower because of the ringgit's rise against the U.S. dollar, traders said on Monday.

"Demand is quite bad. There's not much offtake coming in," a trader for a North American rubber company based in Singapore said. "People are not in a hurry. They feel they can come back after the Chinese New Year."
"Supply is likely to fall in the near-term because of the prolonged rains and a slow down due to the Ramadhan fasting month," one dealer in the Indonesian city of Medan added.
Chinese New Year will be celebrated on February 7 and 8 while Ramadhan ends on February 9. The rubber market has slowed down considerably ahead of the two holidays.
One dealer in Palembang, Indonesia said he was only able to collect between 10 to 15 tonnes of rubber per day, far lower than the usual 25 to 30 tonnes, due to heavy rains.
In Kuala Lumpur, the strong ringgit prompted Malaysian sellers to put in place technical adjustments after the rise in the local currency made domestic rubber more expensive.
"The prices of SMR20 rubber will have to be adjusted lower because of the ringgit's rise against the dollar. The sellers there have no choice in the matter," a Singapore dealer said.

Malaysian traders said buyers, particularly in the Far East, have met most of their rubber requirements for the first quarter of 1997. Fine weather since the start of January had also created comfortable stocks of latex and other raw materials.

"Prices are expected to come off a bit further and this may attract some fresh buying," said one local trader. He said there could eventually be some shortcovering ahead of the Chinese Lunar New Year and Eid al-Fitr festivities in early February.
Traders said prices may rebound after the festivals, when plantations stop tapping rubber for nearly a week and put a strain on the supply of latex to the market.
In the meantime, prices were trending mostly steady to easier, the traders said.

Indonesian benchmark February/March SIR20 offer prices were seen remaining ina range between 54.50-55.00 U.S. cents/lb FOB Medan, 54.25-54.50 FOB Surabaya, Padang and Palembang and at 53.75-54.25 FOB Pontianak and Jambi, dealers said.

The Malaysian Rubber Exchange and Licensing Board quoted the benchmark February RSS1 buyer at 304 Malaysian cents a kg at the close of the market on Friday, against 306.50 cents the previous week. February SMR20 buyer was at 299.50 cents against 304.
Drum latex was offered by trading houses at 237 cents a kg on Friday.
In Thailand, abundant supplies and a quiet market dragged Thai rubber prices down slightly last week, trade sources said.
Thai benchmark RSS3 for February shipment was quoted around US$1.22-$1.23 a kg FOB Bangkok last week compared with the prvious week's $1.23-$1.24.
Latex prices slid to $0.92 a kg on the same basis against the previous $0.93 a kg.
Traders were unsure whether the current soft prices would attract buying interest.
"It also depends on the stock situation and views in major buying countries like Japan," said one Bangkok-based trader.
But industry sources expected prices to firm up from the end of this month onward with the onset of the wintering season when supplies become tight.

"Rubber trees in certain areas, like the northeast have already started wintering. Those in the south will follow. Tapping activities during that time would drop substantially," said Sucharit Promdej of the Thai Rubber Research Institute.
(With contributions from Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia)
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
